::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: ::: {.cell} ::: ## What is a Matrix? ## What can a Matrix Represent? ## What Kinds of Matrices are Useful to us? ### Adjacency Matrix in Networks :::: {.grid} ::: {.g-col-6} Adjacency matrices are a fundamental representation of networks (graphs) in network science. For an undirected graph with $n$ nodes, the adjacency matrix $A$ is an $ n \times n$ symmetric matrix where the columns *and* rows indicate nodes in the network: $$A_{ij} = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if there is an edge between nodes } i \text{ and } j, \\ 0 & \text{otherwise}. \end{cases}$$ For directed graphs, $A$ is generally asymmetric. For weighted graphs, $A_{ij}$ holds the weight of the edge. The matrix encodes the entire topology compactly, enabling linear algebra techniques (matrix powers, decompositions, etc.) to extract insights about structure, dynamics, and function. ::: ::: {.g-col-6} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` V1 V2 V3 V4 V1 0 1 1 0 V2 1 0 1 0 V3 1 1 0 1 V4 0 0 1 0 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-2-1.png){width=2100} ::: ::: ::: :::: ## References ## Content ***Question:*** What is the correspondence, if any, between Adjacency Matrices in Network Science, Karnaugh Maps, Cayley's Group Theory matrices, and Paulus Gerdes' symmetry matrices in Lunda geometry? **There is no single, direct one-to-one correspondence** among all four, but they share deep structural and conceptual overlaps rooted in **binary representations, symmetry, adjacency/operations, and combinatorial geometry**. They are all matrix-like or grid-based tools for encoding relationships, symmetries, or operations. Here’s a breakdown of the connections: ### 1. Adjacency Matrices (Network Science / Graph Theory) - An **n × n** (0,1)-matrix where entry (i,j) = 1 if there is an edge between vertices i and j. - Encodes the **structure of a graph** (who is connected to whom). - Key properties: symmetric for undirected graphs; eigenvalues reveal connectivity, clustering, etc. - Used for random walks, centrality, community detection, etc. ### 2. Cayley Tables (Group Theory) - A square table (matrix) showing the **binary operation** (e.g., multiplication or addition) of a finite group: rows and columns labeled by group elements, entry = result of operation. - For groups like ℤₙ or Klein four-group, it is a **Latin square** with additional algebraic structure (every row/column is a permutation, identity element, inverses). - The **Cayley graph** derived from a group and generating set has an **adjacency matrix** directly built from the group operation (1 if difference is a generator). **Link to adjacency matrices**: Cayley graphs make the group operation visible as a regular graph; its adjacency matrix encodes the algebraic structure. ### 3. Karnaugh Maps (Boolean Algebra / Digital Logic) - A **rearranged truth table** in a grid (usually 2ᵏ cells for k variables) using **Gray code** ordering so that adjacent cells differ by exactly one bit. - Used to **visually group** minterms (1s) or maxterms (0s) for simplification via the adjacency property (Quine-McCluskey idea made graphical). - Not a traditional matrix of relations, but a **geometric encoding of Boolean functions** where spatial adjacency = logical adjacency. **Links**: - To adjacency matrices: The Gray code adjacency reflects Hamming distance 1 (like edges in a hypercube graph). The K-map can be seen as labeling vertices of a hypercube, with 1-regions corresponding to subgraphs. - To Cayley tables: Both use structured grids to reveal algebraic simplifications or closures. Boolean algebras are related to groups/rings in some contexts. ### 4. Paulus Gerdes’ Symmetry Matrices in Lunda Geometry Paulus Gerdes (ethnomathematician) studied **Tchokwe/Lunda sona** (sand drawings) and generalized them into **Lunda-designs** and **mirror curves** — black-and-white patterns with strong **two-color symmetry**, mirror symmetries, and periodic properties. He analyzed these using **matrices** that encode: - Symmetry operations (reflections, rotations, translations). - Coloring rules (e.g., alternating black/white with specific crossing or mirroring properties). - Polyomino-like tilings and **helix matrices**, magic squares, and other combinatorial objects derived from African design traditions. These matrices often exhibit: - **Symmetry axes** (horizontal, vertical, diagonal). - Group-like closure under certain transformations. - Binary (0/1 or black/white) patterns. **Links**: - To adjacency matrices: Lunda patterns can be modeled as graphs (e.g., intersection graphs or dual graphs of curves), with matrices capturing adjacency or incidence. - To Cayley tables / groups: Many Lunda symmetries form or relate to **symmetry groups** (dihedral, etc.). Gerdes explicitly connected his work to group theory and combinatorics. - To Karnaugh maps: Both heavily rely on **binary grids** and **adjacency/symmetry** for simplification or pattern generation. The Gray-code-like local changes in K-maps parallel the smooth, mirror-symmetric transitions in Lunda curves. Both are tools for visualizing combinatorial explosion in a human-readable geometric way. ### Overall Correspondences | Aspect | Adjacency Matrix | Cayley Table | Karnaugh Map | Lunda Symmetry Matrices | |-------------------------|---------------------------|---------------------------|-------------------------------|----------------------------------| | **Core Idea** | Graph connections | Group operation | Boolean function simplification | Cultural symmetry & patterns | | **Structure** | 0-1 matrix | Operation table (Latin sq.) | Gray-code grid | Binary/symmetric pattern matrix | | **Adjacency/Symmetry** | Direct (edges) | Indirect (via generators) | Gray code = logical adj. | Mirror/rotational symmetry | | **Algebraic Flavor** | Spectral graph theory | Group axioms | Boolean algebra | Symmetry groups, tilings | | **Visualization** | Network layout | Multiplication table | 2D map for grouping | Aesthetic black-white designs | **Deep unifying themes**: - **Binary encoding + geometry**: All use grids/matrices to turn abstract relations (connections, operations, truth values, symmetries) into visual, manipulable forms. - **Symmetry and closure**: Groups (Cayley), Boolean functions (K-maps), graphs (adjacency), and Lunda patterns all emphasize invariance under transformations. - **Ethnomathematics ↔ Formal math**: Gerdes’ work bridges African visual traditions with modern graph theory, group theory, and combinatorics — showing how "intuitive" cultural matrices encode the same principles as formal tools. - **Hypercube / Hamming space connections**: K-maps live on hypercubes; Cayley graphs of elementary abelian 2-groups are hypercubes; many Lunda designs have recursive or fractal-like binary symmetry. In short, they are different **representational languages** for the same underlying mathematical universe of **finite structures with symmetry and local-to-global relations**. Gerdes’ Lunda matrices are perhaps the most "visual/aesthetic" bridge, while adjacency matrices and Cayley tables are the most algebraic, and K-maps the most applied (engineering). There is rich potential for further exploration — for example, representing Lunda symmetries as Cayley graphs or using K-map techniques on binary Lunda patterns.
